title: The Biggest Reason You Struggle With Consistency stency/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin argues that the primary, often unrecognized cause of inconsistency in enforcing classroom management plans is not distraction or unclear rules, but simple awkwardness — the discomfort of confronting a student, especially over minor infractions. He offers a four-part system to remove that awkwardness: deliver consequences the same way every time, keep the script simple (state the rule broken and the consequence, nothing more), avoid hesitating or entertaining excuses, and move on immediately without lingering to debate. Linsin compares the ideal posture to a sports referee calling fouls without deliberation. He closes with a concrete practice routine — visualizing common misbehaviors before students arrive and rehearsing the physical act of delivering a consequence — arguing that repeated visualization and rehearsal, not willpower alone, is what makes consistent follow-through automatic.
points: The primary reason teachers struggle with consistency isn't distraction or unclear rules — it's the simple discomfort, or awkwardness, of confronting a student.
A fixed, repeatable script for delivering consequences (state the rule broken, state the consequence, nothing more) removes the need to improvise and reduces discomfort.
Hesitating or entertaining excuses makes every subsequent enforcement harder; the recommended posture is that of a referee calling fouls without deliberation.
Teachers should deliver the consequence and immediately move on, without lingering to argue, explain further, or invite pushback.
Rehearsing the physical act of delivering consequences through visualization before students arrive builds the muscle memory needed for automatic, awkwardness-free follow-through.
quotes: But there is one reason that stands out among the rest. It’s a reason that may have never crossed your mind but is responsible for the majority of teachers who struggle with consistency. It’s awkwardness.
The key is to rely on a system that removes the awkwardness and makes your response to misbehavior automatic. Something you no longer have to think about.
Including any more than that risks causing resentment, an awkward interaction, and greater resistance going forward. It also weakens the effect of the consequence.
It’s best to think of yourself as a referee officiating a game. A student breaks a rule and you call a foul. There is no hesitation or time to waver.
Before your students arrive for the day, close your classroom door, position yourself in front of your room, and visualize your most common misbehaviors.
Practice a few more times, visualizing different behaviors. Just follow the script. And later that day, when a student breaks a rule, you’ll find yourself gliding over without a second thought.
